processing: Nothing specific is documented; Phoenix dancong is generally sun-withered, shaken and rested in rounds, then fixed, rolled and dried.
harvest_season: Not documented; spring is the main picking for Phoenix dancong in general.
appearance_dry: Not described; dancong in general is long, twisted and dark brown.
appearance_liquor: Not described; dancong liquor is usually clear golden to light amber.
appearance_wet: Not described; dancong leaves usually show reddened edges after shaking.
taste_profile: No tasting description is documented. Phoenix dancong as a class is high-aromatic, with floral notes and a returning sweetness.

brewing.notes: General dancong approach only: very hot water and quick pours.

vintage_note: No selling pattern is documented for this name. Phoenix dancong is usually sold by spring harvest of the current year, sometimes with older roasted stock marked by year.
description:
Lao Hama, 'old toad', is a name attached to a Phoenix Mountain dancong, and very little is documented about it. The aroma type, the village and the look of the tree are all unrecorded.

A nickname like this would fit local habit: many Phoenix lines are named after animals and objects. That tells you about the naming custom, not about this tea.

Everything else has to be assumed from the class. Dancong in general is shaken and rested until the leaf edges redden, then brewed very hot and very fast.

If you meet it for sale, ask the seller for the written Chinese name, the village and the aroma type, because the characters themselves are not settled in print.
history: Little is documented: no date, place or person is on record for this name, and it does not appear in the published overviews of Phoenix dancong lines.
